name: Maya Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your name won't be attached to this confidential interview. What do you do on an ordinary day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the lead designer at Fieldline, a six-person agency making signs and printed guides for clinics and performance spaces. This morning I was on the floor of a small theatre, watching people try to find the accessible entrance from a printed map. I have a master's in design and I'm good at catching the gap between what looks clear on a screen and what a visitor can actually follow. My favourite moment is when the usher says fewer people get lost; the worst is a client asking us to remove the testing hours from the quote.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are you paid, and what tools do you use?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I earn about the usual wage for a lead designer here, and I have four months of expenses saved. My partner Imani works variable library shifts; we split the rent, but I don't treat her pay as a guarantee for my half. There are a few other studios and venues nearby, not endless openings. I use AI now and then for rough colour layouts, never for a final route that visitors have to trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the venue manager that small shortcuts are welcome if we keep the real visitor test. A tidy digital map is useful, but the sign has to make sense from the doorway. I'd rather spend our spare hour walking the route than making ten more colours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the clinic and theatre contracts would continue in this mild world. My wage covers my half of rent, and four months saved gives me room if a client pays late. Imani's library shifts vary, so I still like having a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd keep designing paid signs and checking them in the actual buildings. I'd put a fixed amount from each salary payment into savings until the cushion reaches five months. In the first year of this mild change I'd show our director the entrance-test notes when quoting new work, so those hours stay paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The useful part of my work is still there and my own pay looks steady. I would be annoyed if we forgot the person standing in front of a badly placed sign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a test note look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I write down where a first-time visitor hesitates, then photograph the sightline with permission. The theatre's blue arrow looked obvious on my laptop but disappeared beside the blue door. The theatre’s blue-arrow sightline note was worth more than another polished mock-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the four-month cushion enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Enough for an ordinary late invoice or a repair, not forever. Imani and I keep separate savings, so I would not count her account twice. Five months would make a quiet year genuinely easier.

say: I would tell venues a **real visitor test** still matters after minor software shortcuts.
I would spend spare time checking **sign sightlines** rather than making more colour variants.
think: I expect **clinic and theatre contracts** and my wage to continue.
I value **four months saved** because Imani’s library shifts vary.
do: Keep **paid sign design** and test routes inside actual venues.
Transfer a **fixed amount each payday** into savings until expenses have five months of cover.
Show the director **entrance-test notes** when quoting paid testing hours.
feel: **Calm** about steady own pay, with some concern about careless signs.
S0.quote: The theatre’s blue-arrow sightline note was worth more than another polished mock-up.
fieldNote: Her skill lies in **observing people** using signs, not only in attractive layouts.
A four-month reserve and typical pay give **room**, despite variable partner shifts.
She seeks **paid testing time** within current work.

steps.text: Keep designing signs and testing real routes in clinics and theatres
Transfer a fixed amount each salary payment until savings cover five months
Show venue-test notes to the director when quoting paid test hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the agency that AI making layout variants does not make visitor testing free. The three of us on the design team should ask for paid proof and testing time in writing. I would also ask clients to tell us when an automated map actually failed someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think clients will buy fewer of our routine layout hours and Fieldline may cut one design day a week. I could lose paid lead hours even if I still run the difficult tests. Four months saved and Imani's shifts give us time to react, but not a replacement wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This quarter I'd ask the director for paid time to learn the new AI reading-order checker on two actual sign jobs, correcting its flags against visitor notes. I'd join Nia and Pavel from design in a written request to keep paid human testing hours in every automated quote. If my own paid hours fall over the next few years, I'd compare posted venue-wayfinding roles by full-week wages, hours and travel before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can influence how we quote the work, but I cannot promise the client will keep paying for layout time. A one-day cut would be real money for our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Nia and Pavel ask for with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would sign one request together, asking that every AI-assisted venue quote include paid visitor testing and a named person who can correct the map. It is not just me giving a presentation. If the director says no, the three of us can take the same proposal to the next staff meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a venue role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply after my own hours fell if the posting described actual paid access work. I would accept only if its complete weekly wage and hours after travel cover my share of rent, food and bills. A nicer title on a shorter week would not help.

think: I expect clients to buy fewer **routine layout hours**, possibly cutting my paid week.
I see **four months saved** as response time, not a replacement wage.
do: If approved, learn the **new AI reading-order checker** on two paid sign jobs and correct its flags against visitor notes.

feel: **Anxious** about a realistic one-day paid cut, while she can still influence quotes.

fieldNote: Her **new AI test** checks reading order, distinct from occasional colour mock-ups.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the theatre and clinic clients that full thinking AI by 2028 can make a beautiful map, but someone must still try it from the pavement. The robots arrive around 2031, three years later, and may change site checks too. I would ask for written paid testing dates, not a slogan about the human touch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect Fieldline to lose the basic layout contracts quickly, perhaps most of its design income in the first year after 2028. My specialist work might not fill the whole agency's paid week. Four months saved lets us plan, but Imani's library wage cannot carry the whole flat if my pay stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd put my share of rent, food and bills beside Imani's actual recent payslips so we know the gap. I'd keep paid venue projects and ask the two client venues whether they would buy a separate site-walk and sign-correction service. If Fieldline ends my paid design role in the first year after 2028, I'd apply for posted paid venue-access work and compare whole-week wages, hours and travel before accepting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because I can picture most of our income going and I would lie awake over a four-month search. I can ask clients for paid site work, so I am not frozen. I would not tell my partner Imani that a robot delay guarantees my wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the theatre pay for a separate walk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know until the manager signs a price and a date. I would show the notes from a real entrance test and ask for a paid visit, not offer an open-ended free audit. If neither venue buys it, I keep looking for posted work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a venue role involves lifting fixtures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask which signs I'd carry and whether fitting is part of the job. I would take it only if weekly wages and hours after travel cover my share of rent, food and bills. My strength is testing routes, not fitting a high board alone.

I would ask for **written paid dates** for real entrance testing.
think: I expect **basic layout income** to fall sharply at Fieldline.
I know **four months saved** and Imani’s variable wage cannot carry our full rent indefinitely.
do: Compare **rent, food and bills** with Imani’s actual payslips this month.
Keep **paid venue work**; offer two clients site walks with signed price/dates; if neither buys, keep checking posted work.
If role ends in 2028-29, apply for **posted venue access**; accept only for rent/food/bill-covering weekly wages/hours after travel; check fitting duties.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely major income loss despite a four-month search reserve.
S2.quote: I would not tell my partner Imani that a robot delay guarantees my wages.
fieldNote: The **2028 screen loss** comes before capable robots affect site work.
She tests whether **two venues pay** for site walks rather than assuming demand.
She asks about **lifting duties** before acceptance, without a blanket refusal.

steps.text: Compare household rent, food and bills against Imani’s recent library payslips

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our clients that five years is time to test whether real buildings still need paid design visits. A computer may draw the best-looking sign by 2031, but it cannot tell me which doorway a confused visitor actually tries unless someone looks. Robots around 2034 might eventually change even those visits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I can turn my site observation into a service, but the agency has to sell it, not just admire it. I would prefer a paid visit to a new certificate with no client. Five years makes that test possible while my current wages arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting next quarter I'd propose a paid wayfinding walk-through to the clinic and the theatre, using their previous visitor complaints to measure changes. I'd keep my design week while we test whether either client renews the service. In the first year after 2031, if layout work ends and no client renews, I'd compare posted museum or clinic access jobs and apply only where the paid week is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because the current desk can still shrink, but a paid pilot gives me something to measure. If neither client renews, I'll know early enough to use the local openings. A paid renewal tells me more about venue demand than a cheerful meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would do the walk-through?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would go with an usher or receptionist who knows where visitors actually stop, and ask the venue to include both our paid hours in the quote. I would not ask a disabled visitor to do unpaid testing for our portfolio. The client must agree the time and price before we schedule it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave if a museum advert appears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on the advert alone. If our layout work ends, I'd apply for a posted paid opening, then compare its full-week wages and hours after travel with my share of rent and bills before moving. If the pilot renews and pays enough, I may stay with the agency.

I would warn **2031 thinking AI** may draw signs before 2034 robots affect site visits.
think: I see **site observation** as a possible service only if Fieldline sells it.
I need **current design wages** while testing that route.
do: Propose **paid wayfinding walks** to clinic and theatre; schedule only after clients agree time, price and paid staff hours.
Keep **design wages** and record whether either client renews the pilot.
If layout ends in 2031-32 without renewal, apply for **posted access work**; compare weekly wages/hours after travel with rent/bills before moving.
feel: **Anxious**, but a paid pilot makes demand testable before the desk shrinks.
S3.quote: A paid renewal tells me more about venue demand than a cheerful meeting.
fieldNote: The service needs **paid venue agreement**, including staff time, before any visit.
She does not treat **unpaid visitor testing** as a portfolio opportunity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the studio that ten years is enough to keep a record of what actually works in buildings, not just a gallery of pretty screens. We should bargain for the time to test signs and share any productivity savings with the people doing the visits. AGI may draw layouts by 2036; robots around 2039 may later change on-site work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can see several years of useful design work before that, and my own pay looks steady for now. Four months saved is a start, but I would want six before a serious career change. I cannot promise I will still be the lead designer when I am thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd keep leading paid venue projects, put a set amount aside each month toward six months of expenses, and keep our test records with permission. Each autumn I'd check actual posted venue-access wages and hours. In the first year after 2036, if Fieldline ends my role, I'd apply for a posted access job and move only if full-week wages and hours after travel cover my rent and bills; otherwise I'd keep any paid design projects while looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the long future, but my next few years look secure enough to prepare. I would not plan a life around a date on a card. I want six months saved because that is a number I can check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the design team ask for together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nia, Pavel and I would take a signed request to the director for paid site-testing hours and a share of time saved by automated layout. We would ask for a written reply at the staff meeting, not just have me make a technical slide. I cannot promise the director agrees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you count Imani’s pay when considering a move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would put both actual payslips beside the rent, but I would still check whether my new week pays my share. Imani's library hours can change. A decade of warning is not a substitute for a contract with paid hours.

S4.quote: A decade of warning is not a substitute for a contract with paid hours.

Her **shared request** seeks paid testing and benefit from automated time savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it could take the layout contracts before we have sold anything else. A written paid site-testing contract and a real posted venue job with enough hours would help. Four months saved lets me look, but I don't want Imani carrying the rent by herself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets to test a sign. If we only ask the staff who already know every doorway, we will miss the person visiting for the first time. I would like that testing to be paid, including the visitor's time when we ask for it.

headlineQuote: If we only ask the staff who already know every doorway, we will miss the person visiting for the first time.
portrait: Maya is a **27-year-old lead designer** with a master’s degree at a small studio making venue signs and guides.
She uses AI **occasionally** for rough layouts and checks routes with real visitors.
Typical pay, **four months saved** and some nearby openings give her time to test options.
She joins colleagues for **paid testing hours** and tests whether venues will buy site walks.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase layout contracts before the studio sells a replacement service.
whatWouldHelp: A **written paid site contract** and a posted venue role with enough weekly hours.
